notable_claims: Academic freedom principles should be the basis of academic computer policy.
Freedom of expression and the freedom to read are central to the academic mission.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie shares a talk presented to the ACM student chapter at the University of Illinois regarding censorship on the internet. The presentation explores whether universities should carry specific newsgroups like 'alt.sex' and how academic freedom principles should inform computer policy. It draws parallels between library intellectual freedom and the management of public and academic computer facilities.

notable_claims: List creation is restricted to 'officially-recognized' groups or academic classes at Northwestern University.
Technical overhead and machine issues are primary drivers for restricting the creation of small, private mailing lists.

The university grants lists to officially recognized campus groups and academic classes while directing others toward Usenet newsgroups. Requests for small, private social groups are denied due to machine resource constraints.

notable_claims: The university banned newsgroups based on a lack of academic value and presence of pornography.
Banning specific groups may increase network costs if users bypass filters via alternative servers.
classification.summary: The Senate at Johannes Kepler University in Linz, Austria, banned four newsgroups from its network. The university justified the ban by claiming the groups lacked academic or research value and contained degrading pornographic material. It was noted that the ban may have increased network traffic as users sought alternative servers to access the content.

Effective modern activism requires machine-readable voter-registration data.
Digital coordination can overpower the influence of professional lobbyists and special interests.

He argues that digital tools allow individuals to bypass traditional political organizations by coordinating targeted communication campaigns to influence elected officials. notable_claims: Automated bot-posting can transform a free-speech platform into a propaganda channel by flooding groups.
The use of bots creates financial and technical burdens for users who pay for data volume or lack advanced software.
Usenet norms are established by consensus rather than legal definition but are essential for the system's survival.
classification.summary: Jim Bottomley argues that automated bot-posting, specifically by the 'Serdar Argic' entity, does not constitute protected free speech because it drowns out other users and destroys the viability of discussion groups. He contends that relying on individual 'kill files' is insufficient as it places the burden on the victim and excludes users with limited software or paid data plans. The post advocates for collective action and adherence to Usenet norms to prevent the collapse of the network due to bot-driven spam.
classification.title: Semi-FAQ: Kill Files/Argic/Free Speech - some people just don't get it

identity.subject: Semi-FAQ: Kill Files/Argic/Free Speech - some people just don't get it
